source.version: Revised manuscript dated 2023-02-17, explicitly not yet peer reviewed (PDF pp. 1-2).
source.title_on_document: Who Wrote this? How Smart Replies Impact Language and Agency in the Workplace

paper_design_summary: Employees of manufacturing and software companies in Germany completed an online survey on internal company platforms, responding to workplace emails under random assignment to human-written smart replies, AI-generated smart replies, or the same AI replies with time pressure (PDF p. 10, section 3.1). Participants could select a suggested reply or compose their own; the experiment scored response sentiment as a proxy for agency and reported suggestion acceptance, with qualitative interviews of selected experiment participants (PDF pp. 10-14, sections 3.2 and 4.1). The email exercise used artificial conditions, and no creativity or between-person diversity measure was reported (PDF pp. 15-16, section 4.2).

studies.label: Online workplace-email smart-reply experiment with qualitative follow-up

assignment.what_was_assigned: Survey condition: human-written smart-reply suggestions (H-SRs), AI-generated suggestions (AI-SRs), or the same AI suggestions with time constraints (AI-SRs+TC).
assignment.quote: In sum, participants were randomly offered one of three surveys:
assignment.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 9), section 3.1, sentence introducing the survey-condition list.

arms.name: H-SRs
arms.description: Human-written reply suggestions for the twelve emails; participants could instead compose their own response (PDF p. 10, section 3.1).

arms.name: AI-SRs
arms.description: AI-generated reply suggestions for the same twelve emails, without the additional time constraint; participants could instead compose their own response (PDF p. 10, section 3.1).

arms.name: AI-SRs+TC
arms.description: The same AI-generated suggestions, with a few seconds to respond to each email; participants could instead compose their own response (PDF p. 10, section 3.1).

participants.exclusions: One participant was excluded from analysis due to technical problems (PDF p. 11, section 3.3).
participants.who: Employees of two large companies in Germany, one manufacturing and one software, recruited by company email; all wrote German. The paper reports a sample of 346 participants and one exclusion for technical problems, but does not explicitly give the number at randomization, the final analyzed total, or per-arm counts. Count fields are null rather than entering a derived total. Qualitative interviewees were selected from experiment participants.
participants.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 9), section 3.1, population; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 10), section 3.3, sample and technical exclusion; PDF p. 14 (printed p. 13), section 4.1.3, interview subsample.

ai_tool.name_model: AI-generated smart replies; generation provider and model not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: The researcher sent the email texts to a newly created email account, recorded the smart-reply suggestions, and supplied those replies in the surveys. Participants selected a suggestion or typed their own reply; the time-pressure arm received the same AI suggestions. Google Cloud NLP API was the sentiment-scoring tool, not an identified reply generator (PDF p. 10, sections 3.1-3.2).

task.description: Respond to twelve German workplace emails, based on anonymized and shortened real emails, using a suggested reply or composing an independent response; instructions requested participants' own assessment and neutral to moderately agreeing answers when uncertain (PDF p. 10, section 3.1).
task.duration: AI-SRs+TC allowed a few seconds per email; an exact limit and total task duration are not stated (PDF p. 10, section 3.1).

outcomes.name: Mean sentiment of given email responses, used as a proxy for agency
outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: Mean sentiment of given responses: AI-SRs 0.58 versus H-SRs 0.47. Tukey all-pairs HSD q_tukey = 13.05 for H-SRs and AI-SRs; the paper reports significance at the p=0.01 level (df = 342). This is a reported significance level, not an exact pairwise p-value. Whole response texts were scored by Google Cloud NLP API; the unit and aggregation used for the inferential analysis are not explicitly specified, so unit is null. Sentiment does not measure creativity or between-person diversity.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 10), sections 3.2 and 4.1.1; PDF p. 12 (printed p. 11), Figure 4.

company_involvement.description: Nonfinancial involvement by the participating employers: the software company's head of human resources and the manufacturing company's sales director recruited employees; internal company platforms hosted the surveys; the manufacturing head of sales supplied anonymized source emails; software-company employees supplied human-written reply suggestions; and the companies' works councils restricted questions concerning personal work performance. The paper declares no external funding and no conflict of interest.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 8), section 2.4, final paragraph; PDF p. 10 (printed p. 9), section 3.1; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 10), section 3.3; PDF p. 16 (printed p. 15), funding and conflict-of-interest declarations.

eligibility.reason: Core eligibility is no because no creativity or between-person diversity outcome is scored. Random assignment to human-written smart replies, AI-generated smart replies, or the same AI replies with time pressure is explicit (PDF p. 10, section 3.1), although the reply-generation provider and model are not identified. The reported sample of 346 participants and one technical exclusion establish that the study exceeds 50 people; randomized and final analyzed totals are not separately stated and remain null (PDF p. 11, section 3.3). The reported outcomes are response sentiment as an agency proxy, suggestion acceptance, and qualitative experiences (PDF pp. 10-15, sections 3.2 and 4.1-4.2). Language homogenization is discussed as a possible consequence without a measured diversity outcome (PDF p. 15, Table 5). Criterion 3 fails, and the study does not qualify for any context class (creativity-codebook.md, section 3).

one_line_finding: AI-generated suggestions produced higher mean response sentiment than human-written suggestions (0.58 versus 0.47; Tukey q_tukey = 13.05, reported significant at the p=0.01 level; PDF p. 11, section 4.1.1, and p. 12, Figure 4), but creativity and diversity were not measured.

applied.quote: Since sentiment is being used as a proxy measure for agency, evidence amounts to a loss of agency and that AI technology is impacting human responses already.
applied.locator: PDF p. 15 (printed p. 14), section 4.2, hypothesis H2 discussion; PDF pp. 10-13, sections 3.2 and 4.1.1; creativity-codebook.md, section 3, criterion 3.

applied.old: Random allocation to human-written versus explicitly AI-generated reply suggestions is stated (PDF p. 10, section 3.1), although the generation provider and model are not identified. The reported sample of 346 and one technical exclusion establish that the sample exceeds 50 people; the final analyzed total is not separately printed and is not derived here (PDF p. 11, section 3.3). Sentiment is scored on participants' response texts (PDF pp. 10-11, section 3.2). Following the brief's preliminary routing rule for random assignment, a sample above the threshold, and an output-scored outcome, core is unclear and the paper goes to the two-screener pipeline. The codebook's creativity/diversity outcome criterion is nevertheless not met: sentiment and suggestion acceptance do not score creativity or diversity (PDF pp. 11-13, section 4.1.1). Possible language homogenization is discussed rather than measured (PDF p. 15, Table 5).
